facts.text: Oak Hill-Piney was settled by Cherokee families in the 1830s following the Trail of Tears, with further growth along Beatty Creek by the 1870s.
The community's name reflects its landscape of rolling Ozark Highlands terrain characterized by oak-covered hills and pine forests.
Cherokee families built a log meeting house in 1875 that served as a church before becoming a school by 1893.
Economic shifts in the 1930s and 1940s led Oak Hill-Piney toward small-scale logging using the area's abundant oak and pine forests.
The Bureau of Indian Affairs recently transferred the historic Oak Hill-Piney Day School site back to the Cherokee Nation as part of land reclamation.
Beaty Creek forms the southern border of Oak Hill-Piney and serves as a tributary of Spavinaw Creek flowing into Lake Eucha.
